title: The Deal Desk, episode 10: Multiples, and why software is worth three supermarkets
hook: The market pays about twenty-four times EBITDA for software and nine times for grocery chains. Here's why, and how to use multiples without embarrassing yourself.
voice_version: gemini-3.8-flash-tts|Sadaltager|a senior London mergers and acquisitions banker in his late thirties, presenting a finance podcast; slightly lower, deeper register than usual; measured, informative and authoritative, like an FT or Bloomberg presenter explaining to a smart listener; clear and composed, warm but never sarcastic, smug or casual|Autonoe|a curious young university student; bright and engaged, conversational|chunks-v2

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: This is The Deal Desk, episode ten. Today, multiples. The tool bankers use more than any other, and the one most often used badly. Let me start with a professor.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: A professor?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Aswath Damodaran. He teaches valuation at N-Y-U Stern in New York, and every January he publishes free data on how the market values every industry. If you want to understand valuation, his website and his YouTube lectures are the best free resource in the world.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: And what does the data say?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Look at January twenty twenty-six, for American companies with positive EBITDA. Software companies trade at about twenty-four and a half times EBITDA. General utilities, about thirteen and a half times. Grocery and food retailers, about nine times. Brewers and spirits makers, about eight and a half.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: So a euro of software EBITDA is worth nearly three times a euro of supermarket EBITDA.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Exactly. Same euro of profit, completely different price. And one more number to make you suspicious. Car and truck makers: almost forty-eight times.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Forty-eight? Car companies? They make terrible margins.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Which is the lesson. Most car makers trade at low multiples. But that industry figure includes a small number of companies the market prices for huge future growth, Tesla being the obvious one, with an enormous valuation compared with its current earnings. So the average gets dragged up. If you used forty-eight times to value a normal car maker, you'd be wildly wrong. Today: what multiples are, which ones to use, and how not to get fooled.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Okay. Start simple. What is a multiple?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Value divided by a financial metric. Enterprise value over EBITDA. Share price over earnings per share. It tells you how many years of that metric the market is paying for, roughly. Ten times EBITDA means you're paying ten years of today's EBITDA.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: And which ones matter?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Four you must know. E-V over revenue. E-V over EBITDA. E-V over EBIT. And price over earnings, the P-E ratio. Remember the rule from episode eight: enterprise value goes with metrics before interest, equity value with metrics after interest.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Why does E-V over EBITDA get used the most?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Three reasons. It doesn't depend on how the company is financed, because it's before interest. It ignores depreciation, which depends on accounting choices. And EBITDA is a reasonable proxy for operating cash flow. So it's the easiest way to compare similar companies.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: And when would you use E-V over revenue instead?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: When EBITDA is negative or tiny. A young software company losing money has no meaningful EBITDA multiple, so people value it on revenue. But revenue multiples hide differences in profitability. Two companies with the same revenue can have completely different margins.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: And E-V over EBIT?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: When capital intensity differs a lot. EBIT takes depreciation into account. A telecom company that has to keep spending on networks looks cheaper on EBITDA than it really is, because EBITDA ignores that the equipment wears out. EBIT shows that cost.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: And P-E?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: For companies where interest is part of the business. Banks and insurers. For them, enterprise value doesn't really work, because debt is their raw material, not just financing. We'll cover them in week three.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Okay. So, the café chain trades at eight times EBITDA, and another chain at fifteen. The first one's cheaper. Buy it.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: That's the trap, and it's the one interviewers love. A low multiple isn't a bargain by itself. Multiples reflect three things: growth, profitability and risk. A company that grows faster, earns higher returns on its capital, or is less risky deserves a higher multiple. A low multiple often means the market expects slow growth or sees risk you haven't spotted.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Show me with numbers.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Two companies, both with enterprise value of one thousand. Company A has EBITDA of one hundred: ten times. Company B has EBITDA of fifty: twenty times. Looks expensive. But B grows twenty-five percent a year and A doesn't grow at all. In three years, B's EBITDA is roughly ninety-eight. On that number, B is about ten times, the same as A today. So you're paying for B's growth upfront.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: So twenty times can be fair.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: If the growth is real. And that's the whole job of valuation: deciding whether the growth the multiple assumes is believable.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: So why does software trade higher than utilities?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Growth and returns. Software can grow fast without building much: once the code is written, the next customer costs very little. Very high margins and high returns on capital. A utility grows slowly, and it's regulated, so its returns are capped. But it's very stable, which is why it still trades well above supermarkets. Supermarkets have thin margins and fierce competition.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: So I can't compare multiples across industries.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Second trap. Comparing an E-V over EBITDA of a software company with a supermarket tells you nothing useful about which is cheaper. Multiples work when the companies are genuinely comparable: same industry, similar growth, similar size, similar margins. That's tomorrow's topic, trading comparables.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: And when someone says the company trades at twelve times, twelve times what period?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Good question, and it's the third trap. Last twelve months, called L-T-M or trailing, uses the most recent actual year. Forward, or next twelve months, uses analysts' forecasts. For a growing company, the forward multiple is lower, because next year's EBITDA is bigger. If you compare one company's trailing multiple with another's forward multiple, the comparison is broken. Always state which one you mean.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Okay.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: What they'll ask you. First: when would you use E-V over revenue instead of E-V over EBITDA?

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: When the company has negative EBITDA, like an early-stage tech company.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Right. Then add the drawback: revenue multiples ignore margins, so they're only meaningful between companies with similar margin prospects. That second sentence is what separates good candidates.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Second?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Why might two companies in the same industry trade at very different multiples?

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Because one is growing faster?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Give all three drivers. Growth, profitability, and risk. Then give examples: higher expected growth, better margins or returns on capital, lower risk, such as less debt, more recurring revenue, or a stronger market position. Bigger companies often trade at a premium too.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: And third?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: A company trades at fifteen times last year's EBITDA and twelve times next year's. What does that tell you?

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: That EBITDA is expected to grow.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: By how much?

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Fifteen over twelve. About twenty-five percent.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Exactly. You can read the market's growth expectation straight from the two multiples. That's a nice touch in an interview.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Deal of the day?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Last week, Schneider Electric, the French energy management group, agreed to buy Shelly Group, a Bulgarian company that makes smart home devices: small relays and sensors that let you control lights, heating and power from your phone. It's listed on the Bulgarian Stock Exchange and on Frankfurt's Xetra.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: How much?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Seventy euros a share in cash, about one point two billion euros. That's roughly a twenty-seven percent premium to the average share price over the previous six months. The two founders, who own about fifty-seven percent between them, have committed to the deal.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Why does Schneider want it?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Homes are getting more complicated: rooftop solar, heat pumps, home batteries, electric car chargers. Shelly's devices fit into existing homes without rewiring. Schneider wants that in its residential range.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: And the interview question?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Here it is. How would you check whether one point two billion euros is a sensible price for Shelly?

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Compare its multiple with similar companies?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Right, and be structured. First, trading comparables: what similar listed companies trade at, on E-V over EBITDA and, since Shelly is growing fast, E-V over revenue too. Second, precedent transactions: what buyers paid in similar deals, which includes a control premium. Third, a D-C-F, based on Shelly's own cash flow forecasts. And as a sense check, the premium: twenty-seven percent over the six-month average is in the normal range for a takeover. Comps, precedents, D-C-F. That's the trio we'll spend the next ten days on.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Quiz?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Quiz. For you listening. Question one: enterprise value six hundred, EBITDA fifty. What's the E-V over EBITDA multiple? Question two: comparable companies trade at eight times EBITDA. Your target has EBITDA of forty and net debt of one hundred. What's its implied equity value? Question three: a company has negative EBITDA. Which multiple would you use? Question four: share price thirty, earnings per share two. What's the P-E? Question five: enterprise value one thousand two hundred, last year's EBITDA one hundred, next year's one hundred and twenty. What are the trailing and forward multiples?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Pause here if you want to think it through.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Answers. One: twelve times. Two: eight times forty is three hundred and twenty of enterprise value, minus one hundred of net debt, so two hundred and twenty of equity value. Three: E-V over revenue. Four: fifteen times. Five: twelve times trailing, ten times forward.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Question two is the one that matters, isn't it?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: That's literally how a comps valuation works. Multiple, times the target's metric, gives enterprise value, then the bridge back to equity. Tomorrow we do it properly, with Ferrari, and why the market values it like a luxury brand and not a car maker.
